title: YOU THOUGHT GOD FORGOT YOU—BUT ISAIAH 40:31 SAYS SOMETHING FAR MORE POWERFUL THAN “JUST WAIT”
paragraphs: YOU THOUGHT GOD FORGOT YOU—BUT ISAIAH 40:31 SAYS SOMETHING FAR MORE POWERFUL THAN “JUST WAIT”
What “Wait Upon the Lord” Really Means When You’re Tired of Praying, Tired of Hoping, and Starting to Wonder Whether God Still Sees You
There is a kind of tiredness sleep cannot fix.
You can sleep eight hours and wake up carrying it.
You can smile in church with it.
You can worship while carrying it.
You can answer, “I’m okay,” while something inside you quietly whispers…
No, I’m not.
Maybe you have been praying about the same thing for months.
Maybe years.
You prayed when you were hopeful.
You prayed when you were terrified.
You prayed with faith.
You prayed through tears.
Then eventually your prayers became shorter because disappointment had exhausted your vocabulary.
“Lord… please.”
And still, nothing seems to move.
The door remains closed.
The relationship remains broken.
The answer remains unclear.
The grief still hurts.
The temptation keeps returning.
The person you love still has not come back to God.
The breakthrough you thought was coming never arrived.
And somewhere between your first confident prayer and your hundredth exhausted one, a frightening question entered your mind:
God, have You forgotten me?
That question is exactly why Isaiah 40:31 is far more powerful than the inspirational quote we sometimes make it.
Because Isaiah was not speaking to comfortable people who needed a motivational boost.
He was speaking into despair.
And before we reach verse 31, we hear the wounded heart behind the promise:
“Why sayest thou, O Jacob, and speakest, O Israel, My way is hid from the LORD, and my judgment is passed over from my God?” — Isaiah 40:27, KJV
In other words:
God doesn’t see what is happening to me.
God has overlooked my situation.
Maybe heaven has forgotten my name.
Sound familiar?
Then God answers.
Not first by explaining their circumstances.
By revealing Himself.
“Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary?” — Isaiah 40:28, KJV
Read that again slowly.
You are tired.
God is not.
You are confused.
God is not.
You cannot see tomorrow.
God is already Lord over it.
Your strength has limits.
His does not.
And then comes one of Scripture’s most beloved promises:
“But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.” — Isaiah 40:31, KJV
But what does “wait” actually mean?
Because this is where we can misunderstand the verse.
The Hebrew behind the opening phrase is:
וְקוֹיֵי יְהוָה
weqōwê YHWH
Often rendered, “those who wait for the LORD.”
The key idea comes from the Hebrew verb קָוָה — qāvâ.
Depending on context, it carries the sense of waiting, looking for, expecting, or hoping.
That matters.
Biblical waiting is not spiritual laziness.
It is not sitting motionless while refusing responsibility.
It is not pretending pain does not hurt.
It is not manufacturing positive thoughts until God gives you what you ordered.
And it certainly does not mean that if you wait long enough, God is obligated to give you the exact relationship, promotion, healing, opportunity, money, or earthly outcome you requested.
Waiting upon the Lord means your expectation becomes anchored in God Himself.
There is an enormous difference between saying…
“I trust God because I know He will give me what I want”
…and saying…
“I trust God because He is God, even when I do not yet understand what He is doing.”
The first trusts an outcome.
The second trusts the Lord.
And sometimes God allows the outcome to remain uncertain until we discover which one we were actually worshiping.
That hurts.
Because some of us do not merely want God.
We want God plus the answer.
God plus the marriage.
God plus the healing.
God plus the restored relationship.
God plus the successful ministry.
God plus financial security.
God plus the apology.
God plus vindication.
And if God does not give us the thing after His name, our hearts begin wondering whether He is still good.
Isaiah 40 confronts that theology.
The promise is not that those who wait upon God will always receive their preferred circumstances.
The promise is that God Himself supplies strength to people who have reached the end of theirs.
Verse 29 says:
“He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength.”
Notice who qualifies.
The faint.
The powerless.
The exhausted.
Not merely the impressive believer.
Not the person who never struggles.
Not the Christian who always knows exactly what God is doing.
The exhausted person.
That means your weakness is not automatically evidence that God has abandoned you.
Sometimes weakness is the very place where you finally stop pretending you can carry yourself.
Even young people grow exhausted, Isaiah says. Even the naturally strong eventually stumble.
Human strength always reaches a boundary.
God’s does not.
And then Isaiah says those who wait for YHWH will “renew” their strength.
The Hebrew expression is:
יַחֲלִיפוּ כֹחַ
yaḥălîp̄û kōaḥ
They will renew strength.
The verb can carry the idea of changing or renewing. The picture is not that believers suddenly become self-sufficient superheroes.
The source remains God.
You arrive depleted.
He remains inexhaustible.
You arrive saying, “I cannot.”
And sometimes God does not immediately remove the road.
He gives you strength for the next step.
That may be the part of Isaiah 40:31 we overlook.
Everybody loves the eagle.
“They shall mount up with wings as eagles…”
That belongs on posters.
Then comes:
“They shall run, and not be weary…”
Still inspiring.
But finally:
“They shall walk, and not faint.”
Walk?
After flying?
After running?
Why end there?
Perhaps because much of faithful Christianity does not feel like flying.
It feels like walking.
One ordinary obedient step after another.
Getting out of bed when grief says stay there.
Opening Scripture when your emotions feel numb.
Praying when heaven feels silent.
Refusing the pornography again.
Forgiving again.
Repenting again.
Showing up again.
Choosing integrity when compromise would be easier.
Worshiping Christ when nobody applauds.
Trusting God on Tuesday afternoon when there is no dramatic music, no miracle in sight, and no explanation for why the road became this difficult.
Walking.
And not fainting.
Maybe that is the miracle you have been overlooking.
You wanted God to make you fly.
But God has been keeping you walking.
You thought nothing supernatural was happening because the mountain was still there.
Yet somehow, after everything that should have destroyed you…
you are still here.
Still praying.
Still searching.
Still reading this.
Still whispering the name of Jesus.
Maybe with trembling faith.
Maybe with questions.
Maybe with scars.
But still here.
Do not despise that.
Sometimes grace looks less like escaping the fire and more like discovering that Christ did not abandon you inside it.
And this is where Isaiah 40 ultimately directs Christian hearts beyond ourselves.
The Gospel does not tell us that faithful people never suffer.
It gives us Jesus Christ.
Jesus entered suffering.
He knew rejection.
He knew betrayal.
He knew exhaustion.
He knew sorrow.
He knew what it was to be abandoned by friends.
And at Calvary, the sinless Son of God bore the judgment sinners deserve.
Christian hope therefore rests on something infinitely stronger than “things will eventually work out the way I want.”
Our hope rests on a crucified and risen Savior.
Jesus died for our sins.
Jesus was buried.
Jesus rose again.
And because Christ lives, waiting is never ultimately waiting upon an uncertain God.
We know His character most clearly at the cross.
The cross tells the guilty sinner:
God's grace is greater than your scandal.
The resurrection tells the despairing believer:
The darkest chapter does not get to write the ending.
Maybe your greatest waiting problem is not even your circumstances.
Maybe you have been running from God.
Maybe there is secret sin nobody knows about.
Maybe everyone thinks you are spiritually strong, but you know what happens when the door closes and the screen lights up.
Maybe resentment has hardened you.
Maybe pride has quietly replaced prayer.
Maybe you have learned Christian vocabulary without actually surrendering your life to Christ.
Maybe you have been asking God to change your circumstances while He has been confronting your heart.
Then waiting upon the Lord cannot mean merely waiting for God to improve your life.
It means turning toward Him.
Repentance is not paying God back for your sins.
You cannot.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior who paid what you could never pay.
You do not clean yourself enough to become worthy of Jesus.
You come to Jesus because you are not.
That is grace.
Peter failed spectacularly.
Thomas doubted.
Paul once persecuted Christ’s church.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left to repair his reputation.
Yet the Gospel repeatedly shows us a Savior who meets sinners in places respectable religion would rather hide.
That does not make sin insignificant.
It makes grace astonishing.
Jesus does not merely decorate broken lives.
He redeems sinners.
He forgives.
He restores.
He transforms.
He calls us out of darkness and teaches us to walk with Him.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
So perhaps tonight your prayer does not need to be impressive.
Maybe it simply needs to be true.
“Jesus, I am tired.”
“Jesus, I don't understand.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Jesus, I have been trying to control everything.”
“Jesus, I have been trusting the answer more than I have been trusting You.”
“Jesus, teach me to wait.”
That is not weak faith.
Sometimes that is where genuine faith begins.
Waiting upon the Lord means I may cry while I wait.
I may ask questions while I wait.
I may seek wise counsel while I wait.
I may work responsibly while I wait.
I may go to the doctor while I wait.
I may apply for the job while I wait.
I may apologize while I wait.
I may establish necessary boundaries while I wait.
I may lament while I wait.
But underneath all of it remains one stubborn confession:
My hope is in the Lord.
Not because I know exactly what He will do.
Because I know who He is.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, do not manufacture a polished testimony. Be honest.

And if Christ has already carried you through a season you once thought would destroy you, tell someone what He did. Your testimony may become the encouragement another exhausted believer desperately needs tonight.
Not because every day will feel inspiring.
The friend who keeps saying, “I’m fine.”
The believer who is tired.
The person who stopped attending church.
The one wrestling with doubt.
Even the person who does not yet believe in Jesus.
Not to pressure them.
To remind them that there is still hope in Christ.
Supporting Christian ministry financially is not what makes someone faithful, saved, or pleasing to God.
But believers are called to use what God entrusts to them for His glory, and voluntary generosity has always had a place in advancing Gospel work.
If God has used this ministry to strengthen you, and you are able and willing to help us keep placing Christ-centered truth before more people, you can support Gospel Warrior here:
And comment.
Tell us where you are in the waiting.
You do not need to reveal private details.
Just write:
Because somewhere beneath this article, another exhausted believer may see your comment and realize…
I’m not the only one.
And perhaps that is what you needed to hear too.
You are not commanded to understand everything before trusting God.
You are invited to know the One who never grows weary.
So when you cannot fly…
walk.
When you cannot run…
walk.
When yesterday's strength is gone…
wait upon the Lord.
When your prayers seem unanswered…
wait upon the Lord.
When tears keep coming…
wait upon the Lord.
When you cannot see what God is doing…
look again at Jesus Christ.
Look at the cross.
Look at the empty tomb.
Your circumstances may still contain unanswered questions.
But the cross has already answered the greatest question:
Does God love sinners enough to come for them?
Yes.
With nail-pierced hands.
And maybe the sentence you need to carry into tomorrow is simply this:
The God you are waiting for has not grown tired of carrying you.
